sections.title: Annual Fee Review and Periodic Full Benchmarking

blocks.text: PointOak generally conducts a full plan and provider benchmark every three to five years, or sooner when circumstances warrant. In years when we are not conducting a full benchmark, we perform a fee benchmark and work with the provider to reprice the plan annually. The three-to-five-year interval is PointOak's practice, not a DOL or ERISA requirement.

items.q: How much does 401(k) evaluation and benchmarking cost?

a.text: The cost depends on your plan size, participant count, assets, and whether the engagement includes benchmarking alone or full RFP support.

PointOak operates on a fee-only consulting model, so we never receive commissions, revenue sharing, or referral compensation from recordkeepers or investment providers. Fees are based on the scope of work, including provider benchmarking, fee analysis, investment evaluation, fiduciary consulting, or RFP management.

Whether you need a standalone benchmarking engagement or ongoing consulting that includes 3(21) investment fiduciary or 3(38) investment manager services, we'll provide a transparent proposal before work begins. Your initial consultation is complimentary and carries no obligation.

items.q: Should we always choose the lowest-cost 401(k) provider?

a.text: No. ERISA requires fiduciaries to select a provider that is appropriate for the plan—not simply the lowest-priced option.

A prudent evaluation considers service quality, investment flexibility, participant experience, cybersecurity, compliance support, technology, and overall value alongside fees. A provider that charges slightly more may ultimately deliver better outcomes and stronger fiduciary documentation.
PointOak helps committees compare providers objectively using documented scoring criteria rather than focusing on price alone.

items.q: What is an Investment Policy Statement (IPS), and does our plan need one?

a.text: An Investment Policy Statement establishes the framework for selecting, monitoring, watch-listing, and replacing plan investments.

While ERISA does not specifically require an IPS, it has become an industry best practice because it provides consistent standards for investment oversight. Without one, committees often make investment decisions without documented criteria, making fiduciary oversight more difficult to demonstrate.
PointOak helps retirement plan committees develop and maintain Investment Policy Statements that support long-term governance.

items.q: Does participant-directed investing eliminate the sponsor's fiduciary responsibility?

a.text: Even when participants choose their own investments, plan sponsors remain responsible for prudently selecting and monitoring the investment options offered under the plan.

ERISA Section 404(c) provides certain liability protections regarding participant investment decisions, but fiduciaries must still demonstrate a prudent process for selecting, monitoring, and documenting the investment lineup.
PointOak helps committees maintain that documentation through ongoing investment analysis and governance support.

items.q: How important is cybersecurity when evaluating a retirement plan provider?

a.text: Cybersecurity has become an essential fiduciary consideration.

The Department of Labor encourages plan sponsors to evaluate provider security practices as part of the provider selection and monitoring process. We review areas such as SOC reports, encryption standards, incident response procedures, breach notification requirements, insurance coverage, and contractual liability protections.
Cybersecurity is treated as a core evaluation category—not an afterthought.
